query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in air at elevated temperature induces fine, coherent oxide precipitation (primarily TiO2 and/or NiO) within the single-phase titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy, leading to enhanced high-temperature strength and thermal stability compared to untreated material.
generation.material_initial_state: Titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-cast HEA to a pre-oxidation annealing treatment (e.g., heating at approximately 800 °C in a controlled air atmosphere for a defined short duration) prior to final processing or testing.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature or extreme-environment mechanical testing conditions (e.g., temperatures ≥800 °C under static or cyclic loading) in an oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a fine dispersion of nano-scale oxide particles (such as TiO2 and/or NiO) along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nano-oxides act as dispersion-strengthening agents that pin dislocations and stabilize grain boundaries, thereby inhibiting grain growth and enhancing yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy will exhibit higher yield strength, increased hardness, and improved creep resistance under elevated-temperature conditions relative to an identical alloy processed without the pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.baseline: Identical titanium–nickel HEA produced without the pre-oxidation annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents in a single-phase solid solution. It is expected to be beneficial under oxidizing, high-temperature test conditions (around or above 800 °C). However, excessive oxidation, non-optimal treatment temperatures, or durations might compromise ductility or lead to undesirable phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature, time, and atmosphere control needed to achieve the desired oxide dispersion without detrimental effects are uncertain. The precise magnitude of the strength and stability improvements remains to be quantified, and further optimization is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical titanium–nickel HEA samples. Subject one set to the controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment (e.g., 800 °C in air for a specified duration) and leave the other set untreated. Perform identical elevated-temperature mechanical (e.g., tensile, hardness, and creep) tests on both sets in an oxidizing environment (≥800 °C).
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to verify oxide dispersion and grain boundary characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show statistically significant improvements (for example, yield strength increases greater than ~10% and reduced creep rates) compared to the untreated samples, or if excessive oxidation is observed that degrades mechanical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application.
